video_title: Michael Moritz on Origin Stories, Exile, and Obsessive Curiosity
transcript: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome  back to Conversations with Tyler. Today,   I am chatting with Michael Moritz.  Michael is perhaps best known for   his work as a venture capitalist  through Sequoia. Before that,   he was a very active and successful journalist  with several books to his credit, including   the first study of Apple and an excellent  work on Alex Ferguson of Manchester United. Michael is extremely well known, in addition,  for his work in philanthropy. For instance,   his institution Crankstart has  been supporting the Booker Prize   since 2019. He also is involved in San  Francisco Standard, but most importantly,   from our point of view, Michael has a new  and excellent book out called Ausländer:   One Family’s Story of Escape and Exile, which I  absolutely recommend to you all. Michael, welcome. MICHAEL MORITZ: Thank you for that  very kind and flattering introduction. COWEN: I have many questions for you  in many areas. Let’s start with Wales.   Did the nonconformism of Methodist Wales make it  easier for Jews to settle and feel at home there? MORITZ: I’m not sure that that actually was the  case. I think that the principal reason that Jews,   particularly the ones of my parents’ generation,   settled in Wales were that those with  entrepreneurial attributes were encouraged to   settle in South Wales and in some other  parts of Britain to set up businesses,   to encourage local employment, and stimulate job  growth. I don’t think that any aspect, probably of   the established church or churches made the new  immigrants to Wales feel any more comfortable. COWEN: How was Welsh antisemitism  different from English antisemitism? MORITZ: Well, first of all, I want to be really  careful here because Britain opened its doors to   my parents. My parents were refugees from Nazi  Germany. They both were permitted to come into   Britain as children, as teenagers. Both of them  were around 14 years old when they were fortunate   enough to land in Britain. Britain was one of the  few countries, albeit with quotas, that opened   the doors to Jews desperately trying to flee the  Nazi stain that was spreading all over Europe. Britain, back in the late 1930s and certainly  during the time that I was growing up there,   which was predominantly in the 1950s, ’60s,  and early ’70s, was far less a multicultural   country than it is today. Anybody from abroad,  they could have been Italian waiters in Soho—there   were very few blacks or anybody from Asia in  Britain at the time that I was growing up—anybody   who looked out of the ordinary was considered by  the majority of the people, as always happens,   a bit of an outsider. That was displayed in a  whole variety of ways. Nonetheless, whether it was   in Wales or, to answer your question, in England,  I’m not sure that it differed all that much. COWEN: According to some sources,   the population of Welsh Jews peaked  in around 1919 at around 5,000,   and then it declined radically. Why did so many  Jews leave Wales? Is it just movement to London? MORITZ: I don’t think it declined that rapidly.  I think there were, I don’t know how many in the   ’60s when I was growing up, maybe there were 600  families around Wales that were Jewish out of a   population of around, probably back then, about  2.5 million. I think the younger people tended   to leave for opportunity. Small countries or  Wales and other parts of the United Kingdom that   presented limited opportunity for people  with ambition meant that the younger people   in particular tended to leave, and they  tended on the whole to head toward London. COWEN: You left Wales at age 19, correct? MORITZ: Yes, 18, 19. COWEN: What was your thought process  at the time? Was it screaming,   “I have to get out of here,”  or a marginal decision? MORITZ: No, it was far more conventional than  that. I left Wales after I finished high school   and I went to university. That was the first time  I’d lived in England. Then outside of vacations,   I never really went back to Wales. Since 1973,  my life has been really spent outside of Wales. COWEN: At that young age, were you  already interested in art and fiction? MORITZ: Funnily enough, I was in both. Take the  art first. I think I owe this to my mother, whom   otherwise I had a fairly strained relationship  with, but bless her heart. She was the victim   of this age-old prejudice against women and left  school at the age of 15 and always felt a little   inferior to people with college and university  educations. She had a really—and I don’t know,   I never talked to her about it—I don’t know  where it came from. She had a lifelong affection   for the visual arts and for music. At home, the  radio was always on with her listening to music. When she took me and my sister to the museum  in Wales, the National Museum of Wales, which   actually has a pretty good collection, some really  interesting impressionist pictures and, oddly,   some Francis Bacon. I think that’s what woke my  interest in art. I bought my first picture, which   I gave as a gift to my parents when I was 13. I  did so in Cardiff. It was a little watercolor and   pencil drawing of a winding mechanism at a pit  head, these big winding mechanisms that used   to sit astride the places in coal mines in Wales  where the coal came up from below. I still have   that picture. After my mother died, I got it, and  it hangs in my office at home, right by my desk. COWEN: Is it easy to live with an Otto  Dix painting or sketch? It hangs on the   wall. Many people think it’s ugly. It reminds  one of unpleasant things in history, right? MORITZ: Yes, for Harriet and  me it is. I think the tougher,   more strenuous, grueling works of art  that other people would have difficulty   living with have many layers to them. You  explore them, and they’re difficult pictures,   and they’re not easy at first sight. Unlike  easier pictures that may be a bit more decorative,   they leave room for plenty of exploration,  as the years go by. Then they’re redolent,   they tell stories. They’re redolent of history.  They’re images of a different epoch. I think most   of the paintings that we’ve been lucky enough to  find over the years, they are tough paintings. COWEN: I feel that way about Haitian art,   which has many brutal scenes. For  you, is Chagall too sentimental? MORITZ: Yes. COWEN: You don’t want to put it on your wall? MORITZ: The earlier Chagalls I’ve been drawn to,   but neither of us have felt the urge or  the need to go out in pursuit of Chagall. COWEN: What is your own painting like?   MORITZ: Oh, exasperating. COWEN: Neue Sachlichkeit or  something else, it’s like Kossoff? MORITZ: No, I don’t know if you’ve ever tried  painting or drawing. I didn’t take it up until   I was in my mid 40s. I’d never picked up a crayon  or outside of the obligatory, abbreviated art   lessons that always seem to be held later on  Thursday afternoon, with everybody waiting   for the bell to ring to end school. I’d never  taken up a crayon or drew, or let alone painted. If I look back today at what I did early  on, it’s a lot better. Then if I look at   the paintings that I try to make, my goodness,  it is an extremely humbling experience,   but I enjoy it. I really enjoy it. There’s  nothing like getting lost in making a painting,   and before you know it, two hours have gone,  and you have no idea where the time went. COWEN: How has living with the visual  arts improved your investing skills? MORITZ: I’m not sure that it’s had any  influence whatsoever on investments. COWEN: Talent identification, isn’t it some area  where there’s always a deeper understanding in   the visual arts, and you then later can apply  those frameworks to individuals or companies? MORITZ: I understand the argument, but I began  my life as a journalist and maybe subliminally,   because I look fairly intently and always  look fairly intently at works of art that   have caught my eye, I think I’ve always looked  carefully at whatever it is in front of me. It   could be a landscape, could be a building,  could be a person, and have been pretty   watchful and have listened carefully. I think  all three are connected when you are trying to   take the measure of somebody when you’re thinking  about forming a business relationship with them. COWEN: Your father was a classics scholar.  Were you interested in Homer as a teenager? MORITZ: I was not. I suppose, like a lot  of sons, I tried to get as far away from   the classics as possible. My Latin teacher  at school was sure that he had a little   Latin genius on his hands since I was the  son of a classics professor, and then I   proceeded to severely disappoint  him for the next three years. COWEN: What in Jewish literature  means the most to you? MORITZ: Well, when I was growing up, I devoured  the works of the American Jewish authors who   really made their mark during the 1950s and 1960s,  and predominantly Philip Roth and Norman Mailer,   although there is obviously a string of  others as well. Those were the two that,   as soon as they published a new book,  I immediately went out to buy the book. COWEN: You knew Roth, right? What was he like? MORITZ: I was very lucky when I  went to university in America,   I went to the University of Pennsylvania,  and here he was, one of the heroes of modern   literature. He was teaching a small seminar  class at the University of Pennsylvania and I   enrolled in it. And as a teacher, he had edited  a Penguin series on Eastern European authors,   so he taught from that canon. And one of his  abiding virtues as a teacher or as a professor,   was he prescribed short books to read, so he  didn’t ask his students to read 600-page tomes. Most of the books that I remember him  asking us to read were fairly short,   so you could really read them without feeling  out of breath and then have time to ingest them.   And he listened very carefully and was very polite  and courteous toward all of his students. Then   he very, very kindly wrote me a reference  when I applied for a job at Time Magazine.   I’m not sure that many people who applied  at Time had a reference from Philip Roth. Then later in life, way later in life, our  paths crossed again through a mutual friend   and for several years, when our family was in  the habit of going to New York to celebrate   Thanksgiving with friends, Philip was a mutual  friend of the hostess and so for, I don’t know,   half a dozen years, we always had Thanksgiving  dinner and among the guests was Philip Roth. And   unless he was in a deep funk, he was  always wry and amusing and sardonic. COWEN: How would you describe your  current relationship to the Hebrew Bible? MORITZ: More distant than removed. I am not  an observant Jew and haven’t been. I obviously   identify very proudly as a Jew. My father was what  in America would be called a conservative Jew,   and he was deeply educated in the Jewish  Bible and interpretations of the Jewish Bible.   I think maybe his fascination with it, just like  his devotion to Latin, I think drove me away from   it. But he had also grown up in an era in Germany  where there weren’t very many distractions,   and I think the main entertainment of the week,  best as I could tell, was going to the synagogue. COWEN: Why do you think sons and daughters do not   ask more questions about their parents’  and grandparents’ history when they can? MORITZ: They’re too self-absorbed. They aren’t  curious. They don’t understand that every   individual has a story, and on the whole, with  every individual, the more that you dig, the more   interesting it becomes. They don’t know how to  ask questions, and they don’t know how to listen. COWEN: If you could ask your parents  something now, what would you ask? MORITZ: It wouldn’t be one question.  Because I obviously have written this   book that’s a family memoir about what  happened to my parents’ generation,   and how that shaped me. It wouldn’t be one  question, Tyler. It would be hundreds of   questions. And you know better than I do  from all the interviews that you’ve done,   it’s the answer to a question that then prompts  another question. I probably can’t imagine   running out of questions for either of them,  but these are for people who’ve been through   extraordinarily traumatic times. People also  suppress memories. It’s sometimes difficult to,   even though their spirit may be willing,  it’s very difficult to excavate an answer. COWEN: Say it’s your grandparents, Max and Minnie,   who were killed in the Holocaust.  Where would you start with them? MORITZ: I think I’d probably start where I do,  oddly enough, with founders at the beginning,   because right or wrong—and different people will  have different opinions—I just think the first 10,   15 years of life that anybody  experiences shapes the individual   in profound and deep fashions that then  whatever happens to them, subsequently,   echo through their life. It’s really  the details of the circumstances. Imagine being a 10-year-old boy in 1890 or  1891, and you’re in a little village beside   a river in the middle of Germany. Well,  what was life really like? Who woke you   up in the morning? Did you have somebody  else sleeping in the same bedroom or in   the same bed? Do you remember what you  had for breakfast? What were the clothes   that you wore to school? I mean, you can just  think of hundreds and hundreds of questions. Obviously, my grandfather, the gentleman that  you alluded to, Max, he joined the German army,   and he served in World War I and was one of the  survivors of the most gruesome, brutal battle   in the history of mankind, which was Verdun. He  survived it. You can just imagine the number of   questions you’d want to ask about that. That’s  just one experience and obviously an enormously   dramatic experience, but you can just imagine the  number of questions you’d want to ask about that. COWEN: Why do you think it is in the  late 19th century that there’s such   a resurgence of antisemitism  in Germany, which for a while,   at least by many people, was considered  better than average by European standards   on this question? Maybe that was an illusion,  but something strange seems to happen, right? MORITZ: I don’t know that it was in the  19th century, Tyler. I think it was much   more in the early 20th century after the end  of World War I. I think antisemitism in the   late 19th century, with the Dreyfus Affair,  in Western Europe, was far more prevalent   in France than it was in Germany, but I think  probably the influx of refugees from the East,   from Russia, from Ukraine, who  fled West because of the pogroms,   probably didn’t help matters in late  19th- and early 20th-century Germany. Until Bismarck, Germany had always  had very strict—like every other   country under the aegis of the Roman Catholic  Church—they’d had very strict prohibitions against   assimilating Jews. They were only permitted in  Germany—and this dates back hundreds of years.   It wasn’t anything to do with the late 19th  century—in some places, they were only permitted   to live in particular places, but there were a  whole bunch of professions that weren’t available   to them. They were tolerated as itinerants,  as peddlers, as cattle dealers, as merchants. Then, obviously, there were a few who  became the favorite so-called court Jews,   who helped the various monarchs throughout  Germany with their military undertakings,   and helped finance various other exploits, but  they were in a very, very small minority, but   Jews in Germany as for Jews elsewhere, had always  lived on the outside. It was Otto Bismarck who   made life considerably easier for them. Even after  that, they clearly weren’t in the mainstream. COWEN: Why is there such a  resurgence of antisemitism today? MORITZ: Antisemitism has a very long history. It’s  2,000 years old. I think it’s in the atmosphere of   humanity, always has been, always will be. I’m  not complaining about it. I’ve benefited vastly   from being a Jew, so don’t get me wrong, I’m not  whining about it or anything like that. I just   think it’s a condition of the human race, and  I think it flares up in societies where people   feel left behind. They’ve felt that they’ve got a  rough deal. Maybe it flares up too amongst people   who are less well educated and for whom rabble  rousers, who want to point accusatory fingers at   particular people, whether they’re Haitians or  Jews or Somalis, and can stir the pot by doing so. Clearly, social media has made it easier to spread  these sorts of accusations and rumors. I think the   situation in Israel clearly has not helped.  This is obviously well known, and there’s this   obviously amorphous border between not agreeing  with the policies of the Netanyahu government,   which many Jews both in Israel and outside  Israel don’t agree with, and antisemitism.   That, at the moment, I think inflames things  further. It doesn’t help when you have the   mayor of New York say he would arrest Netanyahu  would Netanyahu ever set foot in Manhattan. COWEN: Why are the Irish in particular  so anti-Israel and sometimes antisemitic? MORITZ: I don’t know that. I  just don’t know. First of all,   I don’t know whether it’s true. I don’t  know the stats. I don’t know the data.   I would point out that the only connection between  Ireland and Judaism or Israel that I know about   is that the current president of Israel, his  grandfather was the chief rabbi of Ireland. COWEN: There’s Leopold Bloom  also in Ulysses, of course. MORITZ: There is, yes. COWEN: Now, these days, how is it  you feel when you revisit Germany? MORITZ: I hadn’t been to Germany for a  long time. I went last summer. Oddly,   I’d never been to Munich, which is where my  father grew up and from which my grandparents were   deported and eventually met their death and other  relatives too. Munich today is, on the surface,   like a charming city, very beguiling, the  sort of place one might want to live. Then,   obviously, every corner has a particular history  in Munich, as it does in many European cities. Last summer I went to—I don’t know who the  architect was, I forget—the extremely moving   building that is the new synagogue in Munich.  I actually never go into a synagogue but I   had been curious about attending a service  there. I tried to get into the synagogue,   but because I hadn’t filled out application  forms, because the security was so tight,   because the police were all around it, and because  I didn’t have the documentation to really prove   who I was and hadn’t had authorization to be  admitted, I couldn’t get into the synagogue. Then I went to Dachau, which is not  very far from the center of Munich,   which is where several relatives of mine had been  sent. I did what tourists do and went around it.   Beyond obviously being very aware of the  history of it, the one emotion it stirred   up was when I was standing in a gas chamber.  It was a gas chamber with multiple ovens,   and it was spotless, really, really  clean. Everything was spotless. There were these high school students who were  obviously bored out of their minds on their   iPhones in there and with their AirPod earplugs  in. I just stood there for a moment, shutting   my eyes, wondering what the heat was like, what  the smell was like, what the screams were like,   what the work was like, what the stench was  like. That could have been a million years ago,   but that was the one place that really  struck me, the vast difference between   the scene that I visited and the  scene as it was in the early 1940s. COWEN: The media report [that] you’re  applying for German citizenship? MORITZ: I actually have it. I’ve received it. COWEN: You have it? Congratulations. Where  in Germany do you feel most at home? Munich? MORITZ: I’m not sure that I feel at  home in Germany. People have asked,   why did I apply for German citizenship? Do I  expect to be driven out of the United States?   I have British nationality as well. No,  I don’t. Do I expect to be made to feel   extraordinarily unwelcome and threatened  and terribly frightened in San Francisco?   Absolutely not. Do I envisage a time  where I would be living in Munich? No. The one lesson that I took from working on my  book was you can never have enough passports.   The reason that I applied was, both in Western  Europe and also including the United States,   the one place where the history of  the ’20s and ’30s and the Holocaust   is really drummed into a population is  in Germany. Doesn’t happen in France,   doesn’t happen in England or Wales,  doesn’t happen in the United States. COWEN: Other than a lot of history and, of  course, detail, at the philosophical level,   what else do you feel you learned writing  this book? More passports? What else? MORITZ: Oh, one more. Yes,  on a philosophical level,   I’m not a philosopher, so I  don’t really know what you mean. COWEN: Every venture capitalist  is a philosopher, in my view. MORITZ: Oh, I see. Why is that? COWEN: You have a theory of how the world will  be and a theory of what makes people successful,   however implicit. You couldn’t have  written your Alex Ferguson book if   you were not in some way a philosopher.  It’s about successful organizations,   sustainability, how irascibility can  sometimes make you a better mentor. MORITZ: I think of philosophers as being people  like the great thinkers of the past, Aristotle,   Cicero. I don’t think of writing a book about  leadership as being particularly philosophical.   It’s a summation of observations and lessons.  As I said, I’m no student of philosophy. COWEN: They wrote about exile,  right, and having to leave? MORITZ: Yes, they did, they did. I think  the thing I learned most from writing the   book was it educated me on how I became  what I became, the forces that shaped me,   the influences of my parents, the influences  of the milieu in which I grew up. All of that   shaped who I am, and I understood that a lot  better after I finished working on the book. COWEN: In your life, how exactly is it that you   moved from being a journalist to being  a very successful venture capitalist? MORITZ: There was no plan. It was great  good fortune. I had wound up working in   the San Francisco bureau for Time Magazine.  I worked for Time Magazine for a few years   at the beginning of my professional  life. When I moved to San Francisco,   I really didn’t know anything about Silicon  Valley. I didn’t know anything about the tech   industry or the tech business. Obviously, it was  a lot different and smaller then than it is today. Although I was supposed to write  about all sorts of different topics,   because the bureau in San Francisco covered  pretty much everything from, believe it or not,   Alaska down to Santa Barbara, the  thing that I got attracted by was   Silicon Valley. There were no technology  companies in 1981, ’82 in San Francisco   unless you count Charles Schwab, who had  set up his discount brokerage there. I   got really interested in writing about these  companies, and they were really, really small.   You mentioned earlier that I had written a book  about Apple. I had got to know Apple fairly well,   but at the time it went public, it had sold  about 100,000 computers, 150,000 computers.   It was really tiny, but I then got introduced  through writing about these companies—Atari,   Apple, Microsoft, Oracle, others. I’d never  met anybody in Wales. I’d never conceived of   the idea that anyone would start a company,  let alone anybody who is 18 or 20 years old. Then I began to understand how  some of the mechanics worked,   and I couldn’t start a company. I joined  a company, but it was a little publishing   company that didn’t require any technical skill  or computer science background or electrical   engineering or semiconductor know-how. I  just didn’t have that sort of a background. Through covering these individuals, I then  began to understand that there were these   investors who invested in their companies, so I  started writing. I did a few stories about the   venture capital industry, and I got to meet  several of the then-leaders of the industry,   Tom Perkins, who started Kleiner Perkins, and then  Don Valentine, who started Sequoia. I had quit   Time, had cast my lot with this little publishing  company that many, many years later, thanks to the   co-founder, was bought by Dow Jones, but that  had nothing to do with me. I’d left that too. I literally wrote letters back then—you  couldn’t write emails—to the people who   ran five venture firms, got rejected  by four of them, and then I got really,   really lucky and Don Valentine hired me  at Sequoia. I think when some of his peers   heard that he’d hired a history major who’d  been a journalist who didn’t have an answer   of technical acumen, never worked for a Silicon  Valley company, they thought he’d lost his mind. COWEN: Why not publish your book  on Don Valentine? Rumor has it   there are only a few copies in your Tuscany hotel. MORITZ: It’s not really a book. It’s a  fairly long profile of not just about Don,   it’s about the early venture industry. COWEN: Many people would love to read it, right? MORITZ: That’s kind of you to say that. I’m not  sure that there’s enough in there to merit a book. COWEN: What do most people  get wrong about Steve Jobs? MORITZ: Maybe what a stoic he was and the heroic  manner in which he spent his last years, which I   can barely imagine. The fact that his native wit,  his raw intelligence, the melding of an artist and   a capitalist, I think those are the principal  things that aren’t appreciated about him. Also,   I think the education he received during his years  in the wilderness after he got cast out of Apple. COWEN: If we think of your interest in  Steve Jobs, your book on Alex Ferguson,   the art you buy, that you’ve now  written a book on the Holocaust,   is there some general pattern where trying to  come to terms with really difficult things,   is this a recurring theme in your life?  Learning how to paint, that’s very hard, right? MORITZ: I haven’t really thought about it that  way, but I think life is made richer by having   a challenge that you’re not sure whether you’re  up to conquering. I’ve always been up for that.   Each of these books has really just sprung  out of being curious about something. I’m   not sure that there’s any greater  pattern than unsatisfied curiosity. COWEN: I love Otto Dix, but  most people don’t like Otto Dix. MORITZ: Let me know the next  time you come to San Francisco. COWEN: Great. MORITZ: You’ve got to come, and I’d be  very happy to show you what we live with— COWEN: I’d be delighted to see it. MORITZ: —that other people  wouldn’t want to live with. COWEN: I love Lucian Freud as well, the  greatest painter of flesh ever, perhaps, right? MORITZ: Certainly in the 20th century. COWEN: Yes, maybe Rubens, you could say. MORITZ: No doubt. No doubt. COWEN: You have Frank Auerbach also? MORITZ: Oh, yes, big Frank fan, huge. COWEN: Underrated in the United States, right? MORITZ: Yes, but he’s having  a show at the Metropolitan,   I think it’s in two years, in New York. COWEN: I will go. MORITZ: Oh, spectacular artist. I met  Frank on several occasions. In a way,   you were asking about Steve Jobs a few minutes  ago. Steve, I think most great entrepreneurs,   Bill Gates, Elon Musk, were obsessives.  Frank Auerbach carried his obsession   to new heights. He painted every day of the  year, save for one, which was Christmas Day,   when he treated himself to a day off and went to  Brighton to go to the Brighton Pier on Christmas   Day. Then later in life, he decided that,  actually, the one day he was taking off was   stealing time from painting, so he abandoned his  trips to Brighton. There’s an obsessive for you. COWEN: How would you describe  your greatest obsession? MORITZ: I’m more of a dilettante than an  obsessive because I’ve got too many interests.   This isn’t false modesty on my part.  It really isn’t. I just think each   of these pursuits that I dabble in,  each of them I could do a lot better. COWEN: That could be an obsession too, what  you call dabbling in different pursuits?   MORITZ: Yes, or satisfying curiosity. COWEN: What is it you feel you saw early in  China? Many people thought China would grow,   but the notion that you could invest there and  actually get a profit was arguably the better,   more important insight. Around what  corner did you see to grasp that? MORITZ: I think it was a collective  effort at Sequoia. It wasn’t just me.   I think it was going to visit China and meet  people, see what was happening with your own eyes.   I’ve been to Hong Kong before, but I hadn’t  been to the mainland. Going to the mainland,   where so many preconceptions were washed  away, and gradually beginning to understand,   or understanding fairly quickly, that if you  wanted a country where capitalism was ablaze   in the early 21st century, really ablaze,  it wasn’t in the US, it was in China,   despite what everybody says about the  Communist Party and state control. It was   a country where there was a very skimpy,  if nonexistent, social safety net and where   people had to live or die by either the strength  of their education or their wits. Then as the   years went by and I got better educated about  China, having a far keener appreciation of the   strengths of the country as it came to grips with  what technology had to offer, Sequoia flourished. And I think it was one of the  better decisions that we made   for close to two decades in China, where  it was possible to invest in pretty much   anything anybody wanted to invest in  any industry. It’s tightened up a lot,   obviously, in the last few years, and so the  atmosphere and circumstances are different. COWEN: Through Crankstart,  you’ve been supporting the   Booker Prize. What have you learned doing that? MORITZ: Oh, how little I know about literature.  I don’t read all of the submissions, obviously,   and I have nothing to do with the judging of  the prize whatsoever. It’s as big a mystery   to me as it is to everybody else. I enjoy the  challenge of going through the 12 shortlisted   books that come out in the summer or the  books for the International Booker Prize,   because they just open your eyes new  authors, countries perhaps that you don’t   know very much about, circumstances  that you don’t know too much about.   I try to maintain a balance of reading fiction  and nonfiction, so the Booker keeps me honest. COWEN: Does it feel to you like fiction is in a  pretty good place right now? I argue this to my   friends. They’re often skeptical, but if I think  about Ferrante, Knausgård, the Sonia and Sunny   book, Houellebecq, Cărtărescu, I think there’s  a lot of great works just in the last 10 years. MORITZ: Yes. Oh, I would completely  agree. Douglas Stuart’s one of my   favorite authors as well. Storytelling,  despite what everybody says about AI,   great storytelling is never going to go out  of style, and it begins with words on paper. COWEN: How would you improve the San  Francisco nonprofit community? There’s   a lot of money. There’s going to be a lot  more money. There aren’t that many talented   people to run nonprofits. Is the whole thing  just a mess? Is it doomed? Will it succeed? MORITZ: I think two things. One, it’d be great  to have more people in San Francisco interested   in contributing in some fashion. The second is,  I think, having people from the for-profit world   operating philanthropies is very helpful  and sets a different performance standard. Missy Narula, who’s the wonderful CEO of  Crankstart, her background before she joined us   five years ago was TPG and Bain. It  wasn’t in the not-for-profit world.   She has this wonderful ability to straddle  both worlds. She has the sensibility of a   person who cares deeply about others  and those who are left behind. Also,   the need for performance that comes out of  having spent many years in the for-profit world. I think it’s very easy for people  to point fingers at philanthropies   or not-for-profit services and say that they can  be run more effectively. I think that’s probably   true for lots of them, but you can say the same  for many companies as well. What you try to do,   I think, is set a standard and be the best.  Also, knowing that some of the things that   you’re going to try in philanthropy, just  like in business, are not going to work.   Harriet and I have been so fortunate.  It really is our job to try and help   others who just haven’t had the good luck and  fortune and circumstances that we’ve both had. COWEN: There’s a great history of the  arts in San Francisco: the Beat Poets,   Wayne Thiebaud, Jefferson Airplane, Grateful Dead,   one could go on and on. Are the next  30 or 40 years going to look like that,   or is everyone just priced out? Maybe they’ll  live in Fresno and have a patron in San Francisco. MORITZ: I think that’s quite possible.  Look, we’re working very hard. Daniel Lurie,   the wonderful mayor of the city, is working very  hard to make it far easier to build housing.   If you can’t build housing, and if developers and  people who want to put up new houses are left in   a straitjacket, people are going to be priced  out of the city, no doubt about it. I think   most people are already priced out of the city,  the same as they’ve been priced out of Manhattan. Artists have always needed to go to places where  they can afford to live. I noticed that there was   a piece in the New York Times over the weekend  about Syracuse, New York, being a great haven   for writers. Part of the reason being that  it was affordable and rents were low compared   to New York City and Boston. Look, housing is a  huge problem throughout the country. Housing is,   I think, the biggest issue in California,  and it’s an acute issue in San Francisco. COWEN: Now, your book starts with an  anecdote where about 20 years ago,   you were diagnosed with what is  supposedly an incurable blood cancer,   and yet here you are alive and kicking and  just finished a book. How did it change how   you allocate your time over the last 20 years?  It’s at least some level of uncertainty, right? MORITZ: It made me want to control my own calendar  rather than have others control my calendar. COWEN: Was that good for your efficiency  or just good for your happiness? MORITZ: I think more for my contentment. I’m  not sure that I became any more efficient.   Probably pretty inefficient. I did not  want to be imprisoned by obligations   that only formed part of  the life I wanted to lead. COWEN: How do you distinguish  between true friends and others? MORITZ: I think it’s the ones  you want around your deathbed. COWEN: How do you know which  ones they are, other than family? MORITZ: Oh, there are very few of them.  Through life, I think it’s very difficult   to have deep relationships with a lot of people.  It’s just very hard because it’s built on history,   it’s built on the wavelengths missing,  it’s built on shared experiences,   and there’s just not enough time  to do that with lots of people. COWEN: Why does the United Kingdom seem to  be so stuck now economically, politically,   otherwise? In its most fundamental terms,  what has gone wrong there? There’s a lot   of particular mistakes they’ve made, but  why so much correlation in the mistakes? MORITZ: I think it’s the residue of the arrogance  of empire. Obviously, it’s the mantle. The pound   sterling was the reserve currency 100 years ago  or so and the world’s reserve currency. Britain   had the world’s largest navy, obviously had, for  better or worse, its tentacles all over the world,   and it was the world power. Then the mantle  was lost to an entrepreneurial country. I don’t think Britain has ever recovered from the  loss of the position of primacy. Everything, since   then, has been a somewhat feeble, muted reaction  to it, and where—and there’s a new prime minister   who was appointed very recently, obviously—you’ve  had these cycles where government is all the   answer, and then certainly under the Thatcher  years, and later to a lesser extent, under Blair   and Gordon Brown and David Cameron, years where  government wasn’t seen as the answer. It’s sad to   watch, it’s sad to witness, but I think Britain  overall has suffered from too much government. COWEN: Before my last question, just  to promote your book again, Ausländer:   One Family’s Story of Escape and Exile. I  very much enjoyed reading it. Final question,   what is it you wish to learn about next? MORITZ: Iran. COWEN: How will you do that?  It’s hard to go there, right? MORITZ: I am not talking about  contemporary Iran. I’m talking   about Iran—I don’t know whether  or not I’ll go ahead and do it,   but I’ve been reading a lot about it  recently—circa 1900, 1890 to 1960, 1970. COWEN: The constitutional liberal era, like 1908,   1911. I’m so curious as to what  it was actually like back then. MORITZ: Yes. I do not pretend to a  great degree of deep knowledge about it,   but I am extremely curious because I  think so many of the issues that we   confront today stem back to that period  and to what happened in the early 1950s. COWEN: Michael Moritz, thank you  very much. It’s been a real pleasure. MORITZ: Tyler, you’ve been extremely generous,  and your questions were just wonderful. Thank you. COWEN: Much appreciated.

transcript_segments.text: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome  back to Conversations with Tyler. Today,
I am chatting with Michael Moritz.  Michael is perhaps best known for
his work as a venture capitalist  through Sequoia. Before that,
he was a very active and successful journalist  with several books to his credit, including
the first study of Apple and an excellent  work on Alex Ferguson of Manchester United.
Michael is extremely well known, in addition,  for his work in philanthropy. For instance,
his institution Crankstart has  been supporting the Booker Prize
since 2019. He also is involved in San  Francisco Standard, but most importantly,
from our point of view, Michael has a new  and excellent book out called Ausländer:
One Family’s Story of Escape and Exile, which I  absolutely recommend to you all. Michael, welcome.
MICHAEL MORITZ: Thank you for that  very kind and flattering introduction.
COWEN: I have many questions for you  in many areas. Let’s start with Wales.
Did the nonconformism of Methodist Wales make it  easier for Jews to settle and feel at home there?
MORITZ: I’m not sure that that actually was the  case. I think that the principal reason that Jews,
particularly the ones of my parents’ generation,
settled in Wales were that those with  entrepreneurial attributes were encouraged to
settle in South Wales and in some other  parts of Britain to set up businesses,
to encourage local employment, and stimulate job  growth. I don’t think that any aspect, probably of
the established church or churches made the new  immigrants to Wales feel any more comfortable.
COWEN: How was Welsh antisemitism  different from English antisemitism?
MORITZ: Well, first of all, I want to be really  careful here because Britain opened its doors to
my parents. My parents were refugees from Nazi  Germany. They both were permitted to come into
Britain as children, as teenagers. Both of them  were around 14 years old when they were fortunate
enough to land in Britain. Britain was one of the  few countries, albeit with quotas, that opened
the doors to Jews desperately trying to flee the  Nazi stain that was spreading all over Europe.
Britain, back in the late 1930s and certainly  during the time that I was growing up there,
which was predominantly in the 1950s, ’60s,  and early ’70s, was far less a multicultural
country than it is today. Anybody from abroad,  they could have been Italian waiters in Soho—there
were very few blacks or anybody from Asia in  Britain at the time that I was growing up—anybody
who looked out of the ordinary was considered by  the majority of the people, as always happens,
a bit of an outsider. That was displayed in a  whole variety of ways. Nonetheless, whether it was
in Wales or, to answer your question, in England,  I’m not sure that it differed all that much.
COWEN: According to some sources,
the population of Welsh Jews peaked  in around 1919 at around 5,000,
and then it declined radically. Why did so many  Jews leave Wales? Is it just movement to London?
MORITZ: I don’t think it declined that rapidly.  I think there were, I don’t know how many in the
’60s when I was growing up, maybe there were 600  families around Wales that were Jewish out of a
population of around, probably back then, about  2.5 million. I think the younger people tended
to leave for opportunity. Small countries or  Wales and other parts of the United Kingdom that
presented limited opportunity for people  with ambition meant that the younger people
in particular tended to leave, and they  tended on the whole to head toward London.
COWEN: You left Wales at age 19, correct?
MORITZ: Yes, 18, 19.
COWEN: What was your thought process  at the time? Was it screaming,
“I have to get out of here,”  or a marginal decision?
MORITZ: No, it was far more conventional than  that. I left Wales after I finished high school
and I went to university. That was the first time  I’d lived in England. Then outside of vacations,
I never really went back to Wales. Since 1973,  my life has been really spent outside of Wales.
COWEN: At that young age, were you  already interested in art and fiction?
MORITZ: Funnily enough, I was in both. Take the  art first. I think I owe this to my mother, whom
otherwise I had a fairly strained relationship  with, but bless her heart. She was the victim
of this age-old prejudice against women and left  school at the age of 15 and always felt a little
inferior to people with college and university  educations. She had a really—and I don’t know,
I never talked to her about it—I don’t know  where it came from. She had a lifelong affection
for the visual arts and for music. At home, the  radio was always on with her listening to music.
When she took me and my sister to the museum  in Wales, the National Museum of Wales, which
actually has a pretty good collection, some really  interesting impressionist pictures and, oddly,
some Francis Bacon. I think that’s what woke my  interest in art. I bought my first picture, which
I gave as a gift to my parents when I was 13. I  did so in Cardiff. It was a little watercolor and
pencil drawing of a winding mechanism at a pit  head, these big winding mechanisms that used
to sit astride the places in coal mines in Wales  where the coal came up from below. I still have
that picture. After my mother died, I got it, and  it hangs in my office at home, right by my desk.
COWEN: Is it easy to live with an Otto  Dix painting or sketch? It hangs on the
wall. Many people think it’s ugly. It reminds  one of unpleasant things in history, right?
MORITZ: Yes, for Harriet and  me it is. I think the tougher,
more strenuous, grueling works of art  that other people would have difficulty
living with have many layers to them. You  explore them, and they’re difficult pictures,
and they’re not easy at first sight. Unlike  easier pictures that may be a bit more decorative,
they leave room for plenty of exploration,  as the years go by. Then they’re redolent,
they tell stories. They’re redolent of history.  They’re images of a different epoch. I think most
of the paintings that we’ve been lucky enough to  find over the years, they are tough paintings.
COWEN: I feel that way about Haitian art,
which has many brutal scenes. For  you, is Chagall too sentimental?
MORITZ: Yes.
COWEN: You don’t want to put it on your wall?
MORITZ: The earlier Chagalls I’ve been drawn to,
but neither of us have felt the urge or  the need to go out in pursuit of Chagall.
COWEN: What is your own painting like?
MORITZ: Oh, exasperating.
COWEN: Neue Sachlichkeit or  something else, it’s like Kossoff?
MORITZ: No, I don’t know if you’ve ever tried  painting or drawing. I didn’t take it up until
I was in my mid 40s. I’d never picked up a crayon  or outside of the obligatory, abbreviated art
lessons that always seem to be held later on  Thursday afternoon, with everybody waiting
for the bell to ring to end school. I’d never  taken up a crayon or drew, or let alone painted.
If I look back today at what I did early  on, it’s a lot better. Then if I look at
the paintings that I try to make, my goodness,  it is an extremely humbling experience,
but I enjoy it. I really enjoy it. There’s  nothing like getting lost in making a painting,
and before you know it, two hours have gone,  and you have no idea where the time went.
COWEN: How has living with the visual  arts improved your investing skills?
MORITZ: I’m not sure that it’s had any  influence whatsoever on investments.
COWEN: Talent identification, isn’t it some area  where there’s always a deeper understanding in
the visual arts, and you then later can apply  those frameworks to individuals or companies?
MORITZ: I understand the argument, but I began  my life as a journalist and maybe subliminally,
because I look fairly intently and always  look fairly intently at works of art that
have caught my eye, I think I’ve always looked  carefully at whatever it is in front of me. It
could be a landscape, could be a building,  could be a person, and have been pretty
watchful and have listened carefully. I think  all three are connected when you are trying to
take the measure of somebody when you’re thinking  about forming a business relationship with them.
COWEN: Your father was a classics scholar.  Were you interested in Homer as a teenager?
MORITZ: I was not. I suppose, like a lot  of sons, I tried to get as far away from
the classics as possible. My Latin teacher  at school was sure that he had a little
Latin genius on his hands since I was the  son of a classics professor, and then I
proceeded to severely disappoint  him for the next three years.
COWEN: What in Jewish literature  means the most to you?
MORITZ: Well, when I was growing up, I devoured  the works of the American Jewish authors who
really made their mark during the 1950s and 1960s,  and predominantly Philip Roth and Norman Mailer,
although there is obviously a string of  others as well. Those were the two that,
as soon as they published a new book,  I immediately went out to buy the book.
COWEN: You knew Roth, right? What was he like?
MORITZ: I was very lucky when I  went to university in America,
I went to the University of Pennsylvania,  and here he was, one of the heroes of modern
literature. He was teaching a small seminar  class at the University of Pennsylvania and I
enrolled in it. And as a teacher, he had edited  a Penguin series on Eastern European authors,
so he taught from that canon. And one of his  abiding virtues as a teacher or as a professor,
was he prescribed short books to read, so he  didn’t ask his students to read 600-page tomes.
Most of the books that I remember him  asking us to read were fairly short,
so you could really read them without feeling  out of breath and then have time to ingest them.
And he listened very carefully and was very polite  and courteous toward all of his students. Then
he very, very kindly wrote me a reference  when I applied for a job at Time Magazine.
I’m not sure that many people who applied  at Time had a reference from Philip Roth.
Then later in life, way later in life, our  paths crossed again through a mutual friend
and for several years, when our family was in  the habit of going to New York to celebrate
Thanksgiving with friends, Philip was a mutual  friend of the hostess and so for, I don’t know,
half a dozen years, we always had Thanksgiving  dinner and among the guests was Philip Roth. And
unless he was in a deep funk, he was  always wry and amusing and sardonic.
COWEN: How would you describe your  current relationship to the Hebrew Bible?
MORITZ: More distant than removed. I am not  an observant Jew and haven’t been. I obviously
identify very proudly as a Jew. My father was what  in America would be called a conservative Jew,
and he was deeply educated in the Jewish  Bible and interpretations of the Jewish Bible.
I think maybe his fascination with it, just like  his devotion to Latin, I think drove me away from
it. But he had also grown up in an era in Germany  where there weren’t very many distractions,
and I think the main entertainment of the week,  best as I could tell, was going to the synagogue.
COWEN: Why do you think sons and daughters do not
ask more questions about their parents’  and grandparents’ history when they can?
MORITZ: They’re too self-absorbed. They aren’t  curious. They don’t understand that every
individual has a story, and on the whole, with  every individual, the more that you dig, the more
interesting it becomes. They don’t know how to  ask questions, and they don’t know how to listen.
COWEN: If you could ask your parents  something now, what would you ask?
MORITZ: It wouldn’t be one question.  Because I obviously have written this
book that’s a family memoir about what  happened to my parents’ generation,
and how that shaped me. It wouldn’t be one  question, Tyler. It would be hundreds of
questions. And you know better than I do  from all the interviews that you’ve done,
it’s the answer to a question that then prompts  another question. I probably can’t imagine
running out of questions for either of them,  but these are for people who’ve been through
extraordinarily traumatic times. People also  suppress memories. It’s sometimes difficult to,
even though their spirit may be willing,  it’s very difficult to excavate an answer.
COWEN: Say it’s your grandparents, Max and Minnie,
who were killed in the Holocaust.  Where would you start with them?
MORITZ: I think I’d probably start where I do,  oddly enough, with founders at the beginning,
because right or wrong—and different people will  have different opinions—I just think the first 10,
15 years of life that anybody  experiences shapes the individual
in profound and deep fashions that then  whatever happens to them, subsequently,
echo through their life. It’s really  the details of the circumstances.
Imagine being a 10-year-old boy in 1890 or  1891, and you’re in a little village beside
a river in the middle of Germany. Well,  what was life really like? Who woke you
up in the morning? Did you have somebody  else sleeping in the same bedroom or in
the same bed? Do you remember what you  had for breakfast? What were the clothes
that you wore to school? I mean, you can just  think of hundreds and hundreds of questions.
Obviously, my grandfather, the gentleman that  you alluded to, Max, he joined the German army,
and he served in World War I and was one of the  survivors of the most gruesome, brutal battle
in the history of mankind, which was Verdun. He  survived it. You can just imagine the number of
questions you’d want to ask about that. That’s  just one experience and obviously an enormously
dramatic experience, but you can just imagine the  number of questions you’d want to ask about that.
COWEN: Why do you think it is in the  late 19th century that there’s such
a resurgence of antisemitism  in Germany, which for a while,
at least by many people, was considered  better than average by European standards
on this question? Maybe that was an illusion,  but something strange seems to happen, right?
MORITZ: I don’t know that it was in the  19th century, Tyler. I think it was much
more in the early 20th century after the end  of World War I. I think antisemitism in the
late 19th century, with the Dreyfus Affair,  in Western Europe, was far more prevalent
in France than it was in Germany, but I think  probably the influx of refugees from the East,
from Russia, from Ukraine, who  fled West because of the pogroms,
probably didn’t help matters in late  19th- and early 20th-century Germany.
Until Bismarck, Germany had always  had very strict—like every other
country under the aegis of the Roman Catholic  Church—they’d had very strict prohibitions against
assimilating Jews. They were only permitted in  Germany—and this dates back hundreds of years.
It wasn’t anything to do with the late 19th  century—in some places, they were only permitted
to live in particular places, but there were a  whole bunch of professions that weren’t available
to them. They were tolerated as itinerants,  as peddlers, as cattle dealers, as merchants.
Then, obviously, there were a few who  became the favorite so-called court Jews,
who helped the various monarchs throughout  Germany with their military undertakings,
and helped finance various other exploits, but  they were in a very, very small minority, but
Jews in Germany as for Jews elsewhere, had always  lived on the outside. It was Otto Bismarck who
made life considerably easier for them. Even after  that, they clearly weren’t in the mainstream.
COWEN: Why is there such a  resurgence of antisemitism today?
MORITZ: Antisemitism has a very long history. It’s  2,000 years old. I think it’s in the atmosphere of
humanity, always has been, always will be. I’m  not complaining about it. I’ve benefited vastly
from being a Jew, so don’t get me wrong, I’m not  whining about it or anything like that. I just
think it’s a condition of the human race, and  I think it flares up in societies where people
feel left behind. They’ve felt that they’ve got a  rough deal. Maybe it flares up too amongst people
who are less well educated and for whom rabble  rousers, who want to point accusatory fingers at
particular people, whether they’re Haitians or  Jews or Somalis, and can stir the pot by doing so.
Clearly, social media has made it easier to spread  these sorts of accusations and rumors. I think the
situation in Israel clearly has not helped.  This is obviously well known, and there’s this
obviously amorphous border between not agreeing  with the policies of the Netanyahu government,
which many Jews both in Israel and outside  Israel don’t agree with, and antisemitism.
That, at the moment, I think inflames things  further. It doesn’t help when you have the
mayor of New York say he would arrest Netanyahu  would Netanyahu ever set foot in Manhattan.
COWEN: Why are the Irish in particular  so anti-Israel and sometimes antisemitic?
MORITZ: I don’t know that. I  just don’t know. First of all,
I don’t know whether it’s true. I don’t  know the stats. I don’t know the data.
I would point out that the only connection between  Ireland and Judaism or Israel that I know about
is that the current president of Israel, his  grandfather was the chief rabbi of Ireland.
COWEN: There’s Leopold Bloom  also in Ulysses, of course.
MORITZ: There is, yes.
COWEN: Now, these days, how is it  you feel when you revisit Germany?
MORITZ: I hadn’t been to Germany for a  long time. I went last summer. Oddly,
I’d never been to Munich, which is where my  father grew up and from which my grandparents were
deported and eventually met their death and other  relatives too. Munich today is, on the surface,
like a charming city, very beguiling, the  sort of place one might want to live. Then,
obviously, every corner has a particular history  in Munich, as it does in many European cities.
Last summer I went to—I don’t know who the  architect was, I forget—the extremely moving
building that is the new synagogue in Munich.  I actually never go into a synagogue but I
had been curious about attending a service  there. I tried to get into the synagogue,
but because I hadn’t filled out application  forms, because the security was so tight,
because the police were all around it, and because  I didn’t have the documentation to really prove
who I was and hadn’t had authorization to be  admitted, I couldn’t get into the synagogue.
Then I went to Dachau, which is not  very far from the center of Munich,
which is where several relatives of mine had been  sent. I did what tourists do and went around it.
Beyond obviously being very aware of the  history of it, the one emotion it stirred
up was when I was standing in a gas chamber.  It was a gas chamber with multiple ovens,
and it was spotless, really, really  clean. Everything was spotless.
There were these high school students who were  obviously bored out of their minds on their
iPhones in there and with their AirPod earplugs  in. I just stood there for a moment, shutting
my eyes, wondering what the heat was like, what  the smell was like, what the screams were like,
what the work was like, what the stench was  like. That could have been a million years ago,
but that was the one place that really  struck me, the vast difference between
the scene that I visited and the  scene as it was in the early 1940s.
COWEN: The media report [that] you’re  applying for German citizenship?
MORITZ: I actually have it. I’ve received it.
COWEN: You have it? Congratulations. Where  in Germany do you feel most at home? Munich?
MORITZ: I’m not sure that I feel at  home in Germany. People have asked,
why did I apply for German citizenship? Do I  expect to be driven out of the United States?
I have British nationality as well. No,  I don’t. Do I expect to be made to feel
extraordinarily unwelcome and threatened  and terribly frightened in San Francisco?
Absolutely not. Do I envisage a time  where I would be living in Munich? No.
The one lesson that I took from working on my  book was you can never have enough passports.
The reason that I applied was, both in Western  Europe and also including the United States,
the one place where the history of  the ’20s and ’30s and the Holocaust
is really drummed into a population is  in Germany. Doesn’t happen in France,
doesn’t happen in England or Wales,  doesn’t happen in the United States.
COWEN: Other than a lot of history and, of  course, detail, at the philosophical level,
what else do you feel you learned writing  this book? More passports? What else?
MORITZ: Oh, one more. Yes,  on a philosophical level,
I’m not a philosopher, so I  don’t really know what you mean.
COWEN: Every venture capitalist  is a philosopher, in my view.
MORITZ: Oh, I see. Why is that?
COWEN: You have a theory of how the world will  be and a theory of what makes people successful,
however implicit. You couldn’t have  written your Alex Ferguson book if
you were not in some way a philosopher.  It’s about successful organizations,
sustainability, how irascibility can  sometimes make you a better mentor.
MORITZ: I think of philosophers as being people  like the great thinkers of the past, Aristotle,
Cicero. I don’t think of writing a book about  leadership as being particularly philosophical.
It’s a summation of observations and lessons.  As I said, I’m no student of philosophy.
COWEN: They wrote about exile,  right, and having to leave?
MORITZ: Yes, they did, they did. I think  the thing I learned most from writing the
book was it educated me on how I became  what I became, the forces that shaped me,
the influences of my parents, the influences  of the milieu in which I grew up. All of that
shaped who I am, and I understood that a lot  better after I finished working on the book.
COWEN: In your life, how exactly is it that you
moved from being a journalist to being  a very successful venture capitalist?
MORITZ: There was no plan. It was great  good fortune. I had wound up working in
the San Francisco bureau for Time Magazine.  I worked for Time Magazine for a few years
at the beginning of my professional  life. When I moved to San Francisco,
I really didn’t know anything about Silicon  Valley. I didn’t know anything about the tech
industry or the tech business. Obviously, it was  a lot different and smaller then than it is today.
Although I was supposed to write  about all sorts of different topics,
because the bureau in San Francisco covered  pretty much everything from, believe it or not,
Alaska down to Santa Barbara, the  thing that I got attracted by was
Silicon Valley. There were no technology  companies in 1981, ’82 in San Francisco
unless you count Charles Schwab, who had  set up his discount brokerage there. I
got really interested in writing about these  companies, and they were really, really small.
You mentioned earlier that I had written a book  about Apple. I had got to know Apple fairly well,
but at the time it went public, it had sold  about 100,000 computers, 150,000 computers.
It was really tiny, but I then got introduced  through writing about these companies—Atari,
Apple, Microsoft, Oracle, others. I’d never  met anybody in Wales. I’d never conceived of
the idea that anyone would start a company,  let alone anybody who is 18 or 20 years old.
Then I began to understand how  some of the mechanics worked,
and I couldn’t start a company. I joined  a company, but it was a little publishing
company that didn’t require any technical skill  or computer science background or electrical
engineering or semiconductor know-how. I  just didn’t have that sort of a background.
Through covering these individuals, I then  began to understand that there were these
investors who invested in their companies, so I  started writing. I did a few stories about the
venture capital industry, and I got to meet  several of the then-leaders of the industry,
Tom Perkins, who started Kleiner Perkins, and then  Don Valentine, who started Sequoia. I had quit
Time, had cast my lot with this little publishing  company that many, many years later, thanks to the
co-founder, was bought by Dow Jones, but that  had nothing to do with me. I’d left that too.
I literally wrote letters back then—you  couldn’t write emails—to the people who
ran five venture firms, got rejected  by four of them, and then I got really,
really lucky and Don Valentine hired me  at Sequoia. I think when some of his peers
heard that he’d hired a history major who’d  been a journalist who didn’t have an answer
of technical acumen, never worked for a Silicon  Valley company, they thought he’d lost his mind.
COWEN: Why not publish your book  on Don Valentine? Rumor has it
there are only a few copies in your Tuscany hotel.
MORITZ: It’s not really a book. It’s a  fairly long profile of not just about Don,
it’s about the early venture industry.
COWEN: Many people would love to read it, right?
MORITZ: That’s kind of you to say that. I’m not  sure that there’s enough in there to merit a book.
COWEN: What do most people  get wrong about Steve Jobs?
MORITZ: Maybe what a stoic he was and the heroic  manner in which he spent his last years, which I
can barely imagine. The fact that his native wit,  his raw intelligence, the melding of an artist and
a capitalist, I think those are the principal  things that aren’t appreciated about him. Also,
I think the education he received during his years  in the wilderness after he got cast out of Apple.
COWEN: If we think of your interest in  Steve Jobs, your book on Alex Ferguson,
the art you buy, that you’ve now  written a book on the Holocaust,
is there some general pattern where trying to  come to terms with really difficult things,
is this a recurring theme in your life?  Learning how to paint, that’s very hard, right?
MORITZ: I haven’t really thought about it that  way, but I think life is made richer by having
a challenge that you’re not sure whether you’re  up to conquering. I’ve always been up for that.
Each of these books has really just sprung  out of being curious about something. I’m
not sure that there’s any greater  pattern than unsatisfied curiosity.
COWEN: I love Otto Dix, but  most people don’t like Otto Dix.
MORITZ: Let me know the next  time you come to San Francisco.
COWEN: Great.
MORITZ: You’ve got to come, and I’d be  very happy to show you what we live with—
COWEN: I’d be delighted to see it.
MORITZ: —that other people  wouldn’t want to live with.
COWEN: I love Lucian Freud as well, the  greatest painter of flesh ever, perhaps, right?
MORITZ: Certainly in the 20th century.
COWEN: Yes, maybe Rubens, you could say.
MORITZ: No doubt. No doubt.
COWEN: You have Frank Auerbach also?
MORITZ: Oh, yes, big Frank fan, huge.
COWEN: Underrated in the United States, right?
MORITZ: Yes, but he’s having  a show at the Metropolitan,
I think it’s in two years, in New York.
COWEN: I will go.
MORITZ: Oh, spectacular artist. I met  Frank on several occasions. In a way,
you were asking about Steve Jobs a few minutes  ago. Steve, I think most great entrepreneurs,
Bill Gates, Elon Musk, were obsessives.  Frank Auerbach carried his obsession
to new heights. He painted every day of the  year, save for one, which was Christmas Day,
when he treated himself to a day off and went to  Brighton to go to the Brighton Pier on Christmas
Day. Then later in life, he decided that,  actually, the one day he was taking off was
stealing time from painting, so he abandoned his  trips to Brighton. There’s an obsessive for you.
COWEN: How would you describe  your greatest obsession?
MORITZ: I’m more of a dilettante than an  obsessive because I’ve got too many interests.
This isn’t false modesty on my part.  It really isn’t. I just think each
of these pursuits that I dabble in,  each of them I could do a lot better.
COWEN: That could be an obsession too, what  you call dabbling in different pursuits?
MORITZ: Yes, or satisfying curiosity.
COWEN: What is it you feel you saw early in  China? Many people thought China would grow,
but the notion that you could invest there and  actually get a profit was arguably the better,
more important insight. Around what  corner did you see to grasp that?
MORITZ: I think it was a collective  effort at Sequoia. It wasn’t just me.
I think it was going to visit China and meet  people, see what was happening with your own eyes.
I’ve been to Hong Kong before, but I hadn’t  been to the mainland. Going to the mainland,
where so many preconceptions were washed  away, and gradually beginning to understand,
or understanding fairly quickly, that if you  wanted a country where capitalism was ablaze
in the early 21st century, really ablaze,  it wasn’t in the US, it was in China,
despite what everybody says about the  Communist Party and state control. It was
a country where there was a very skimpy,  if nonexistent, social safety net and where
people had to live or die by either the strength  of their education or their wits. Then as the
years went by and I got better educated about  China, having a far keener appreciation of the
strengths of the country as it came to grips with  what technology had to offer, Sequoia flourished.
And I think it was one of the  better decisions that we made
for close to two decades in China, where  it was possible to invest in pretty much
anything anybody wanted to invest in  any industry. It’s tightened up a lot,
obviously, in the last few years, and so the  atmosphere and circumstances are different.
COWEN: Through Crankstart,  you’ve been supporting the
Booker Prize. What have you learned doing that?
MORITZ: Oh, how little I know about literature.  I don’t read all of the submissions, obviously,
and I have nothing to do with the judging of  the prize whatsoever. It’s as big a mystery
to me as it is to everybody else. I enjoy the  challenge of going through the 12 shortlisted
books that come out in the summer or the  books for the International Booker Prize,
because they just open your eyes new  authors, countries perhaps that you don’t
know very much about, circumstances  that you don’t know too much about.
I try to maintain a balance of reading fiction  and nonfiction, so the Booker keeps me honest.
COWEN: Does it feel to you like fiction is in a  pretty good place right now? I argue this to my
friends. They’re often skeptical, but if I think  about Ferrante, Knausgård, the Sonia and Sunny
book, Houellebecq, Cărtărescu, I think there’s  a lot of great works just in the last 10 years.
MORITZ: Yes. Oh, I would completely  agree. Douglas Stuart’s one of my
favorite authors as well. Storytelling,  despite what everybody says about AI,
great storytelling is never going to go out  of style, and it begins with words on paper.
COWEN: How would you improve the San  Francisco nonprofit community? There’s
a lot of money. There’s going to be a lot  more money. There aren’t that many talented
people to run nonprofits. Is the whole thing  just a mess? Is it doomed? Will it succeed?
MORITZ: I think two things. One, it’d be great  to have more people in San Francisco interested
in contributing in some fashion. The second is,  I think, having people from the for-profit world
operating philanthropies is very helpful  and sets a different performance standard.
Missy Narula, who’s the wonderful CEO of  Crankstart, her background before she joined us
five years ago was TPG and Bain. It  wasn’t in the not-for-profit world.
She has this wonderful ability to straddle  both worlds. She has the sensibility of a
person who cares deeply about others  and those who are left behind. Also,
the need for performance that comes out of  having spent many years in the for-profit world.
I think it’s very easy for people  to point fingers at philanthropies
or not-for-profit services and say that they can  be run more effectively. I think that’s probably
true for lots of them, but you can say the same  for many companies as well. What you try to do,
I think, is set a standard and be the best.  Also, knowing that some of the things that
you’re going to try in philanthropy, just  like in business, are not going to work.
Harriet and I have been so fortunate.  It really is our job to try and help
others who just haven’t had the good luck and  fortune and circumstances that we’ve both had.
COWEN: There’s a great history of the  arts in San Francisco: the Beat Poets,
Wayne Thiebaud, Jefferson Airplane, Grateful Dead,
one could go on and on. Are the next  30 or 40 years going to look like that,
or is everyone just priced out? Maybe they’ll  live in Fresno and have a patron in San Francisco.
MORITZ: I think that’s quite possible.  Look, we’re working very hard. Daniel Lurie,
the wonderful mayor of the city, is working very  hard to make it far easier to build housing.
If you can’t build housing, and if developers and  people who want to put up new houses are left in
a straitjacket, people are going to be priced  out of the city, no doubt about it. I think
most people are already priced out of the city,  the same as they’ve been priced out of Manhattan.
Artists have always needed to go to places where  they can afford to live. I noticed that there was
a piece in the New York Times over the weekend  about Syracuse, New York, being a great haven
for writers. Part of the reason being that  it was affordable and rents were low compared
to New York City and Boston. Look, housing is a  huge problem throughout the country. Housing is,
I think, the biggest issue in California,  and it’s an acute issue in San Francisco.
COWEN: Now, your book starts with an  anecdote where about 20 years ago,
you were diagnosed with what is  supposedly an incurable blood cancer,
and yet here you are alive and kicking and  just finished a book. How did it change how
you allocate your time over the last 20 years?  It’s at least some level of uncertainty, right?
MORITZ: It made me want to control my own calendar  rather than have others control my calendar.
COWEN: Was that good for your efficiency  or just good for your happiness?
MORITZ: I think more for my contentment. I’m  not sure that I became any more efficient.
Probably pretty inefficient. I did not  want to be imprisoned by obligations
that only formed part of  the life I wanted to lead.
COWEN: How do you distinguish  between true friends and others?
MORITZ: I think it’s the ones  you want around your deathbed.
COWEN: How do you know which  ones they are, other than family?
MORITZ: Oh, there are very few of them.  Through life, I think it’s very difficult
to have deep relationships with a lot of people.  It’s just very hard because it’s built on history,
it’s built on the wavelengths missing,  it’s built on shared experiences,
and there’s just not enough time  to do that with lots of people.
COWEN: Why does the United Kingdom seem to  be so stuck now economically, politically,
otherwise? In its most fundamental terms,  what has gone wrong there? There’s a lot
of particular mistakes they’ve made, but  why so much correlation in the mistakes?
MORITZ: I think it’s the residue of the arrogance  of empire. Obviously, it’s the mantle. The pound
sterling was the reserve currency 100 years ago  or so and the world’s reserve currency. Britain
had the world’s largest navy, obviously had, for  better or worse, its tentacles all over the world,
and it was the world power. Then the mantle  was lost to an entrepreneurial country.
I don’t think Britain has ever recovered from the  loss of the position of primacy. Everything, since
then, has been a somewhat feeble, muted reaction  to it, and where—and there’s a new prime minister
who was appointed very recently, obviously—you’ve  had these cycles where government is all the
answer, and then certainly under the Thatcher  years, and later to a lesser extent, under Blair
and Gordon Brown and David Cameron, years where  government wasn’t seen as the answer. It’s sad to
watch, it’s sad to witness, but I think Britain  overall has suffered from too much government.
COWEN: Before my last question, just  to promote your book again, Ausländer:
One Family’s Story of Escape and Exile. I  very much enjoyed reading it. Final question,
what is it you wish to learn about next?
MORITZ: Iran.
COWEN: How will you do that?  It’s hard to go there, right?
MORITZ: I am not talking about  contemporary Iran. I’m talking
about Iran—I don’t know whether  or not I’ll go ahead and do it,
but I’ve been reading a lot about it  recently—circa 1900, 1890 to 1960, 1970.
COWEN: The constitutional liberal era, like 1908,
1911. I’m so curious as to what  it was actually like back then.
MORITZ: Yes. I do not pretend to a  great degree of deep knowledge about it,
but I am extremely curious because I  think so many of the issues that we
confront today stem back to that period  and to what happened in the early 1950s.
COWEN: Michael Moritz, thank you  very much. It’s been a real pleasure.
MORITZ: Tyler, you’ve been extremely generous,  and your questions were just wonderful. Thank you.
COWEN: Much appreciated.
